title: Toward a Perceptual Theory of Transparency
authors: Manish Singh and Barton L. Anderson, 2002
research_question: When does the visual system initiate the percept of one surface seen through another? How does it assign surface properties to a transparent layer?

participants.description: 3 observers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, two naive to the experiment's purposes, and one author.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated beyond 'participated in the experiment'.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Circular disk with a vertically oriented sinusoidal grating (background) on a black background. A smaller disk (target disk) was placed inside the large disk. Near disparity (8.3 min of arc) was introduced to the boundary of the small disk to create a percept of a small homogeneous transparent filter floating in front of a high-contrast grating. Luminance range and mean luminance were varied across experiments.

measures.construct: Perceived transmittance (opacity) of the transparent disk
measures.instrument: Adjustment of luminance range in a matching display

measures.construct: Perceived lightness of the transparent disk
measures.instrument: Adjustment of mean luminance in a matching display
Adjustment of luminance range to indicate 'clearly generates' vs. 'clearly does not generate' transparency

measures.construct: Subjective difficulty and variability of matching task

findings.antecedent: Mean luminance within the matching disk (for transmittance matching)
findings.consequent: Luminance range set to match perceived transmittance
findings.mechanism: The visual system uses relative Michelson contrast to assign transmittance, which is influenced by mean luminance.
findings.quote: as the mean luminance within the matching disk increases, observers set a higher luminance range to match the perceived transmittance

findings.antecedent: Michelson contrast within the target disk
findings.consequent: Slope of linear fits for transmittance matches
findings.mechanism: The visual system uses Michelson contrast to assign transmittance.
findings.quote: as the contrast within the target disk increases, so do the slopes of these linear fits.

findings.antecedent: Metelli's model prediction for transmittance matches (expressed as luminance range)
findings.mechanism: Metelli's model predicts independence, but this prediction is not borne out perceptually by the raw data.
findings.quote: This solution predicts that the transmittance matches...should be independent of mean luminance. Clearly, this prediction is not borne out perceptually.

findings.antecedent: Perceived transmittance matches (expressed as Michelson contrast)
findings.mechanism: The visual system uses Michelson contrast, not luminance range, to assign perceived transmittance.
findings.quote: each of the data curves becomes essentially independent of mean luminance. This is precisely what one would expect from the matches

findings.antecedent: Transparent surface darkens the underlying surface (mean luminance in transparency region < mean luminance in surround)
findings.mechanism: Perceived transmittance depends on both its physical attributes and those of the surface it partially occludes.
findings.quote: Observers systematically overestimate the transmittance of darkening transparent surfaces

findings.antecedent: Transparent surface lightens the underlying surface (mean luminance in transparency region > mean luminance in surround)
findings.mechanism: Perceived transmittance depends on both its physical attributes and those of the surface it partially occludes.
findings.quote: they systematically underestimate the transmittance of lightening transparent surfaces.

findings.antecedent: Black episcotister (generates higher Michelson contrast than white episcotister)
findings.mechanism: The ratio-of-contrasts rule for alpha (transmittance) provides an account for why black episcotisters appear more transmissive.
findings.quote: a black episcotister looks more transmissive than a white episcotister... The ratio-of-contrasts rule for a...provides a simple and complete account

findings.antecedent: Lightness-matching task
findings.mechanism: Lightness computation involves more variables (mean luminance, transmittance) than transmittance computation (two contrast values).
findings.quote: Observers reported the lightness-matching task to be much less natural and substantially more difficult.

findings.antecedent: Lightness matches (iso-lightness curves)
findings.consequent: Convergence toward mean luminance of the surround
findings.mechanism: Observers only partially discount the underlying layer's contribution to lightness.
findings.quote: the matches of Observer M.S. exhibit some degree of convergence toward the mean luminance of the surround

findings.antecedent: Metelli's solution for T (lightness of transparent layer)
findings.mechanism: Metelli's model overestimates the extent of discounting of the underlying layer.
findings.quote: the extent of convergence is considerably weaker than that predicted by the solution for T.

findings.antecedent: Lightness matches
findings.consequent: Bias toward mean luminance in the region of transparency
findings.mechanism: Incomplete discounting of the underlying surface's contribution to lightness.
findings.quote: their matches are biased strongly toward the mean luminance in the region of transparency.

findings.antecedent: Effective luminance F (Gerbino et al., 1990) as a predictor for lightness matches
findings.mechanism: The effective luminance model fails to capture the qualitative trend in the lightness-matching data.
findings.quote: effective luminance fails to capture even the qualitative trend in the lightness-matching data

findings.antecedent: Luminance range lowered in the region of transparency (R-C+ regime)
findings.mechanism: Metelli's magnitude constraint (lowered luminance range) is not sufficient to initiate transparency perception.
findings.quote: observers do not perceive transparency in the regime R-C+ even though luminance range was lowered relative to the surround

findings.antecedent: Michelson contrast increased in the region of transparency (R-C+ regime)
findings.mechanism: Increased Michelson contrast prevents transparency perception, even if luminance range is lowered, supporting Michelson contrast as a critical variable.
findings.quote: observers consistently failed to see transparency in the regime R-C+ even though luminance range was lower... and their data curves followed closely the oblique prediction line based on lowering Michelson contrast.

findings.antecedent: Transparent layers that darken the underlying surface
findings.consequent: Ease and reliability of transparency judgments
findings.mechanism: Asymmetry in visual processing for darkening vs. lightening transparent layers, possibly linked to shadow mechanisms.
findings.quote: judgments of transparency are easy and reliable for darkening transparent layers but difficult and more variable for lightening layers.

findings.antecedent: Lower Michelson contrast in the central disk relative to the surround
findings.mechanism: The visual system uses changes in Michelson contrast as a critical image property to initiate transparency.
findings.quote: Michelson contrast is a critical variable that the visual system uses to initiate the perceptual construction of transparency.

findings.antecedent: Transparent layers that lighten the underlying surface
findings.consequent: Ease and reliability of transparency judgments
findings.mechanism: Asymmetry in visual processing for darkening vs. lightening transparent layers.
findings.quote: For lightening filters...observers reported that the decision as to whether or not the central region is transparent was considerably more difficult.

findings.antecedent: Textural continuity between low-contrast and high-contrast regions
findings.mechanism: The image must be consistent with a generic view of the underlying surface continuing behind a transparent layer.
findings.quote: the textures in the center and surround are continuous with each other, and this display is thus consistent with a generic view

findings.antecedent: Nongeneric or accidental alignments of the transparent layer with underlying contours
findings.mechanism: The visual system rejects unstable or accidental interpretations of image data based on the principle of genericity.
findings.quote: viewing conditions that involve nongeneric or accidental alignments of the transparent layer with underlying contours can prohibit the percept

findings.antecedent: Translucent layer (scattering light)
findings.consequent: Blurring of contours and textures on underlying surfaces
findings.mechanism: Light scattering properties of translucent media cause blurring.
findings.quote: A translucent layer that scatters light in addition to absorbing some proportion of it also makes the contours and textures on the underlying surface appear more fuzzy.

findings.antecedent: Translucent layer (scattering light) causing blurred contours
findings.mechanism: The figural criterion for initiating scission must be extended to include textural continuity modulo blurring.
findings.quote: Observers still perceive transparency in this display...even though the textures in the center and surround are not continuous by the strict criterion

findings.antecedent: Central region appears as transparent disk overlying high-contrast background (contrast-contrast displays, Figure 20a, c)
findings.mechanism: Transparency perception involves decomposition into two separate layers in depth.
findings.quote: the central regions in Figure 20, a and c, appear as transparent disks overlying high-contrast backgrounds

findings.antecedent: Central region appears as opaque disk (contrast-contrast displays, Figure 20b, d)
findings.mechanism: Lack of transparency perception means the central region does not decompose into two separate layers.
findings.quote: the central region in Figure 20d does not similarly decompose into two separate layers.

findings.antecedent: Diamond seen as a transparent surface overlying four white disks (stereo display, Figure 22)
findings.mechanism: Part of the diamond's lightness is attributed to the underlying white disks, causing the diamond itself to appear darker.
findings.quote: the diamond appears darker when it is seen as a transparent surface

findings.antecedent: Diamond seen as an opaque surface viewed through four portholes (stereo display, Figure 22)
findings.mechanism: Without transparency, no discounting of underlying surface lightness occurs, making the diamond appear lighter.
findings.quote: the diamond appears darker when it is seen as a transparent surface than when it is seen as opaque.

findings.antecedent: Texture patch and its surround differ in spatial frequency by more than one octave (contrast-contrast displays)
findings.mechanism: Transparency description provides a computational rationale for the dependence of contrast-contrast on spatial parameters.
findings.quote: the magnitude of the effect is greatly diminished when the texture patch and its surround differ in spatial frequency by more than one octave.

findings.antecedent: Gratings in texture patch and surround have the same orientation (contrast-contrast displays)
findings.mechanism: Transparency description provides a computational rationale for the dependence of contrast-contrast on spatial parameters.
findings.quote: the induction is strongest when the gratings in the texture patch and its surround have the same orientation

findings.antecedent: Gratings in texture patch and surround are perpendicular (contrast-contrast displays)
findings.mechanism: Transparency description provides a computational rationale for the dependence of contrast-contrast on spatial parameters.
findings.quote: weakest when they are perpendicular.

findings.antecedent: Gratings in texture patch and surround have the same phase (contrast-contrast displays)
findings.mechanism: Transparency description provides a computational rationale for the dependence of contrast-contrast on spatial parameters.
findings.quote: the induction is greatest when the gratings in the texture patch and its surround have the same phase

findings.antecedent: Gratings in texture patch and surround are completely out of phase (contrast polarity reversed) (contrast-contrast displays)
findings.mechanism: Transparency description provides a computational rationale for the dependence of contrast-contrast on spatial parameters.
findings.quote: weakest when they are completely out of phase (i.e., contrast polarity reversed).

findings.antecedent: Lateral inhibition as an explanation for contrast-contrast and brightness phenomena
findings.mechanism: Lateral inhibition performs image processing but does not account for surface-level representations, leading to insufficient explanations and incorrect predictions.
findings.quote: The insufficiency of lateral inhibition in the contrast domain is not surprising, given that lateral inhibition has been shown to be similarly incomplete

findings.antecedent: Perceptual construction of transparency (scission)
findings.mechanism: A scission account predicts the correct sign and aspects of the size of the illusion, where lateral inhibition fails.
findings.quote: a scission account predicts not only the correct sign but also certain aspects of the size of the illusion

mechanisms: Visual system decomposes light intensities into separate contributions to infer intrinsic surface attributes.
Visual system uses relative Michelson contrast to initiate percepts of transparency and to assign quantitative degrees of opacity to transparent surfaces.
Incomplete discounting of underlying layers' contributions when judging the lightness of a transparent layer.
The principle of genericity (or nonaccidentalness) for scene interpretation, where the visual system rejects unstable or accidental interpretations of image data.
Asymmetry in visual processing for darkening vs. lightening transparent layers, possibly linked to mechanisms for computing shadows.
Textural continuity (modulo blurring) as a figural grouping cue for initiating perceptual scission.
Perceptual scission (decomposition into layers) as a mechanism for explaining contrast-contrast and brightness illusions.
moderators: Mean luminance of the transparent layer relative to the surround (darkening vs. lightening filters)
Spatial frequency difference between texture patch and surround
Orientation of gratings in texture patch and surround
Phase of gratings in texture patch and surround
Relative depth placement of perceived surfaces

tables.description: Summary of Model Fits for the 3 Observers in Experiment 1 (transmittance matching). Shows linear fit slopes and R² values for different test contrasts.
Predicted and Observed Slopes for the 3 Observers in Experiment 2 (lightness matching). Compares Metelli's predicted slopes to observed slopes.

limitations: Metelli's model assumes balanced transparency (homogeneous transmittance and reflectance), which is not always ecologically valid.
Metelli's model assumes background consists of only two distinct-reflectance regions, limiting its applicability to natural scenes.
Metelli's model assumes uniform illumination, which is often not the case in real environments.
The lightness matching task was reported as difficult and variable, suggesting it is prone to strategic influences from observers.
Current figural grouping criteria do not fully account for blurring effects of translucent filters that scatter light.
The study primarily used achromatic stimuli, limiting generalizability to chromatic transparency.
The focus was on local scission of image intensity, not broader global grouping effects that might also lead to transparency reports.
